longformArticle.deck: A single-event Legend Origins record centered on the 1815 Tambora eruption and the short chain in which sulfur-laced atmospheric reports became a local weather warning cue.
opening: On 10 April 1815, Mount Tambora erupted violently. The immediate sequence is tightly bounded: eruption event, atmospheric anomaly reports, and short-term regional weather disruption.
This record follows that chain and shows how smell and air-quality observations moved from operational notes into later shorthand weather warning language.

storyBody.heading: Eruption and Initial Atmospheric Signals
paragraphs: The sequence begins with the eruption itself. Contemporary notes connect the event to sensory and visual shifts in air quality across the region in the same period.

The earliest layer is practical rather than prophetic: reports of unusual air character, dust-saturated wind, and altered light conditions arrived with routine logistics, shipping, and community notes.
That order is important. The anchor is not a legend claim, but a physical event followed by immediate observation.

storyBody.heading: Port Notebooks and Sea-Wind Reports
paragraphs: Maritime and coastal records copied the unusual air cues quickly, often alongside tide and vessel timing details. In this stage, the smell cue was one operational marker among many others.
Because it was written in log and notice form, the cue became shareable across distances without waiting for memory decay.
The record chain was still short: a notable smell, then observed instability in local conditions, then practical caution.

storyBody.heading: Dry-Season Memory and Crop Fears
paragraphs: In the months after the eruption’s immediate phase, regional memory linked the same scent-memory sequence with unseasonable weather stress and poorer planting timing.
Local language compressed this into a pragmatic warning form: unusual wind-smell and atmospheric taste could justify tightening routine decisions.
The mechanism remained unclear to many residents at the time, so repetition mattered more than full causation.

storyBody.heading: From Observation to Proverb
paragraphs: At the social translation stage, the sequence moved into oral shorthand. A full note became a portable caution phrase and lost some technical detail.
This was the transition from observation record to local warning lore: the same sequence persisted, while explanatory depth narrowed.
The warning phrase did not erase the event history; it made the event usable as a memory marker.

storyBody.heading: Press Sheets and Urban Copies
paragraphs: Newspaper and public notice circulation then widened the shorthand. Reproduction pressure tends to shorten language and preserve memorable sequence points.
Each copy helped the motif travel beyond firsthand observers by retaining only the most repeatable elements.
This is a key folklore mechanism: sequence stability creates cultural persistence.

storyBody.heading: Scientific Aftershock and Legacy Clarification
paragraphs: Later climate science identifies volcanic aerosols, sulfur compounds, and broader atmospheric effects as the core physical drivers behind the observed conditions and prolonged weather anomalies.
That does not invalidate the local memory chain; it separates it from causal certainty and places the smell in its material context.
For Legend Origins, the lesson is clear: preserve the primary chain first, then mark the layer where observation becomes omen language.
